abstracts.abstract: We present a novel algorithmic framework for maintaining graph connectivity in dynamic streams with insertions only, achieving a significant departure from conventional approaches. Traditional single-pass streaming algorithms for graph connectivity require Ω(n polylog n) space, where n denotes the number of vertices, due to the fundamental difficulty of compressing connectivity information. Our framework introduces the concept of hierarchical sparsification, which decomposes the graph into a multi-level structure capturing connectivity at different scales. We prove that this decomposition enables us to maintain connectivity using O(n log n) bits of space while processing each edge in amortized O(log n) time. The key insight is that not all connectivity certificates need to be preserved at full resolution; instead, we strategically collapse redundant information across hierarchy levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework naturally extends to handle vertex arrivals and failures, providing the first dynamic connectivity algorithm with sublinear space complexity in the vertex failure model. Our results establish new lower bounds showing that any single-pass streaming algorithm for 2-edge connectivity must use Ω(n) bits, thereby characterizing the exact threshold where our technique becomes necessary.

We present improved algorithms for the online bipartite matching problem on planar graphs, substantially reducing the competitive ratio gap between known upper and lower bounds. The classic greedy algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 1/2, while the optimal deterministic algorithm reaches 1 - 1/√2 ≈ 0.293. Our main contribution is a deterministic online algorithm with competitive ratio 0.354, improving upon the previous best bound of 0.337. The algorithm employs a novel weighted potential function that captures both the structural properties of planar graphs and the temporal dynamics of online requests. We introduce the concept of regional fairness, which ensures that vertices in well-connected regions receive proportionally more matching opportunities. The analysis leverages the planar dual graph properties to establish a refined charging scheme that tracks resource flow more precisely than previous approaches. Additionally, we prove that no deterministic algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio exceeding 0.367 on planar graphs, narrowing the optimality gap significantly. Our techniques also yield improvements for bounded-degree planar graphs and graphs with bounded treewidth.

We present GraphFlow, a distributed graph processing system designed for iterative algorithms on billion-scale graphs with dynamic updates. Existing distributed graph processing systems such as Pregel and PowerGraph operate on static snapshots, requiring complete graph recomputation when edges are inserted or deleted. GraphFlow introduces a streaming computation model that maintains iterative algorithm results incrementally across dynamic edge insertions. The system architecture consists of three novel components: (1) a distributed dynamic graph store supporting efficient edge updates with O(log n) amortized update latency, (2) a change propagation engine that tracks how local modifications affect global convergence, and (3) an adaptive convergence detector that exploits temporal locality in update patterns. Our experimental evaluation on real-world graphs with up to 500 million edges demonstrates that GraphFlow processes edge updates 15x faster than recomputation-based systems while maintaining algorithm accuracy within 0.1% of full recomputation. The system supports PageRank, connected components, and label propagation with provable convergence guarantees. We open-source the complete implementation, which runs on commodity cloud infrastructure.

We present an optimized implementation of cache-oblivious algorithms for sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) that achieves superior performance across memory hierarchies. While cache-oblivious algorithms offer optimal theoretical guarantees without explicit cache parameter knowledge, their practical performance often lags behind cache-aware implementations due to poor constant factors and irregular memory access patterns. Our approach introduces three key optimizations: (1) a hybrid blocking strategy that combines fine-grained blocking for cache levels with register blocking for the lowest level, (2) an analytical model for predicting optimal block sizes based on matrix structural properties, and (3) a preprocessing phase that restructures the sparse matrix representation to improve spatial locality without increasing storage overhead. Our implementation achieves a 2.8x speedup over the previous best cache-oblivious SpMV implementation and reaches 75-90% of the performance of highly tuned cache-aware codes on standard benchmark matrices. We provide a complete library with automatic tuning capabilities that selects optimal parameters for each input matrix. Experimental results on Intel Skylake and AMD Zen2 processors demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse matrix families including social networks, web graphs, and scientific simulations.
